mcqs.question: What is the core move that turns Two Sum from an O(n²) nested-loop problem into an O(n) one-pass problem?
options: Sorting the array before scanning it once
Comparing every previous element individually against the current element
Using two separate hashmaps, one built from each half of the array
Computing the value that would complete the pair for the current element and checking whether that value was already seen
mcqs.explanation: The complement (target minus the current value) is what would complete the pair, and checking a map for it turns a search into an O(1) lookup — that's the whole insight. No sorting or split-map step is involved.

mcqs.question: In the one-pass Two Sum solution, why does the code check the map for the complement before inserting the current element into it?
options: Checking before inserting prevents an element from being incorrectly paired with itself
Inserting before checking is required to make the lookup O(1)
The order doesn't matter — both orders give equivalent results
Checking after inserting is necessary to record every index correctly
mcqs.explanation: If you inserted first, an element whose complement equals itself (e.g. target is double the value) would match against its own just-inserted entry. Checking first keeps the map limited to strictly earlier elements, and lookup speed is unaffected by the order.

mcqs.question: Two Sum is given `nums = [3, 3]` and `target = 6`. Why does the check-before-insert order correctly return indices (0, 1) instead of matching index 0 against itself?
options: Because duplicate values are removed from the map before pairing
Because the map only stores the first occurrence of any value, ignoring later duplicates
Because indices are hashed instead of values, so duplicates can never match
Because the map at any point only reflects strictly earlier indices, so a value can never be paired against itself
mcqs.explanation: At index 1, the complement 3 is already in the map from index 0 — an earlier, distinct index — so the pair is valid. The map isn't deduplicated or hashed by index; it simply hasn't seen the current index yet when the check runs.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't a hashmap complement lookup directly solve a "find the pair closest to (but not necessarily equal to) the target" variant?
options: A hashmap solves closest-to-target lookups in O(1) using a nearest-neighbor hash
Frequency maps are required for any "closest" style problem
A hashmap has no notion of ordering, so "closest to target" needs a sorted array with two pointers to converge instead
Closest-to-target problems always reduce to counting exact-sum pairs
mcqs.explanation: A hashmap only answers exact membership questions; "closest" needs the ability to move toward the target from both directions, which requires an ordering — exactly what a sorted array and two pointers provide. Hashmaps don't support nearest-neighbor queries.

mcqs.question: When does a hashmap complement lookup clearly beat a sorted two-pointer approach for a pair-sum problem?
options: When the problem requires the original array indices in the answer, since the map naturally stores them while sorting loses original positions
When the array is already sorted and O(1) extra space is required
When the problem asks for the closest pair rather than an exact match
Whenever n is small enough that O(n squared) time is acceptable
mcqs.explanation: Recovering original indices after sorting requires carrying index metadata through the sort, which the hashmap gives you for free by design. The other scenarios described favor the sorted two-pointer approach instead.

mcqs.question: How does the O(n²) solution to 4Sum II apply the complement-lookup pattern to four separate arrays?
options: It sorts all four arrays and applies four-pointer convergence
It only produces a correct count when all four arrays are identical
It computes every quadruple's sum directly with a four-way nested loop across all arrays
It precomputes pairwise sums of two arrays into a frequency map, then looks up the negated pairwise sum of the other two arrays against it
mcqs.explanation: Building a sum-to-count map from the first two arrays in O(n²), then checking each pairwise sum from the remaining two arrays against its negated complement, mirrors Two Sum's complement check applied one level up — pairs of pairs instead of single elements. Nothing here requires sorting or identical arrays.
